title: Using custom Python classes in your Streamlit app
heading: Patterns to define your custom classes
summary: The section explains the behavior of class definitions in Streamlit apps, specifically how defining a class in a separate module prevents it from being redefined on each script rerun, allowing `isinstance()` checks to consistently return `True`. It also discusses the implementation of a custom `__eq__` method in classes, such as `MyDataclass`, to enable value-based comparisons rather than instance-based comparisons, ensuring that equality checks remain valid across reruns. Key features and API names involved include `st.session_state`, `isinstance()`, and the `__eq__` method.

title: Using custom Python classes in your Streamlit app
heading: Understanding how Python defines and compares classes
summary: The section explains the behavior of class definition and comparison in Python, particularly focusing on how redefining a class can lead to unexpected results when comparing instances created from different definitions. It highlights that in Streamlit, the rerun logic can mimic this behavior, where an instance stored in `st.session_state` may be compared to a newly defined class instance, leading to confusion due to differing in-memory IDs. The relevant features and API involved include `st.session_state` and the concept of class redefinition.

title: Using custom Python classes in your Streamlit app

It highlights that the value returned by `st.selectbox` is based on an `Iterable` saved during a previous execution, which can lead to unexpected comparison results when using custom classes that implement identity checks in their comparison operators, such as `__eq__`.

title: Using custom Python classes in your Streamlit app

It details that without this feature, different instances of the same `Enum` class would be treated as unique, causing comparison issues, and introduces the `enumCoercion` setting in the `config.toml` file to manage this behavior.

title: Python pickle serialization constraints

title: Python pickle serialization constraints
heading: What can be pickled and unpickled?[¶](#what-can-be-pickled-and-unpickled)
summary: This section explains the constraints on what can be pickled and unpickled in Python, detailing the types of objects that are picklable, such as built-in constants, numbers, strings, collections, functions, classes, and instances with a picklable `__getstate__()` method. It also describes the exceptions that may arise, specifically `PicklingError` for unpicklable objects and `RecursionError` for highly recursive structures, and emphasizes that functions and classes are pickled by their fully qualified names, not by their code or attributes.
